\chapter{Seasons}
\label{ch:ka-seasons}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the four seasons in Kannada, including the monsoon that actually shapes the Karnataka year.}

Say \kn{ಬೇಸಿಗೆ}, \kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ} and \kn{ಚಳಿಗಾಲ} from native roots, then the doubly-Sanskrit \kn{ವಸಂತ} \kn{ಋತು} for spring.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vasanta ṛtu bēsige maḷegāla caḷigāla]{\kn{ವಸಂತ} \kn{ಋತು}, \kn{ಬೇಸಿಗೆ}, \kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ}, \kn{ಚಳಿಗಾಲ} — native words, plus a double Sanskrit loan}

\label{lesson:KA-C14-kaalagalu}



\begin{quote}
Kannada's summer, rain, and cold words are native, just like Tamil's — but its word for \textquotedblleft{}spring\textquotedblright{} borrows \textbf{twice} from Sanskrit, not once.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Kannada} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ವಸಂತ} \kn{ಋತು}} (\emph{vasanta ṛtu}) & \textquotedblleft{}spring\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{both} \emph{vasanta} AND \textbf{\kn{ಋತು}} \emph{ṛtu} (\textquotedblleft{}season\textquotedblright{}) are Sanskrit \\
\textbf{\kn{ಬೇಸಿಗೆ}} (\emph{bēsige}) & \textquotedblleft{}summer\textquotedblright{} & native Dravidian \\
\textbf{\kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ}} (\emph{maḷegāla}) & \textquotedblleft{}rainy season\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{\kn{ಮಳೆ}} \emph{maḷe}, native Dravidian (\textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\kn{ಕಾಲ}} \emph{kāla} (\textquotedblleft{}time,\textquotedblright{} itself a Sanskrit loan) \\
\textbf{\kn{ಚಳಿಗಾಲ}} (\emph{caḷigāla}) & \textquotedblleft{}winter/cold season\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{\kn{ಚಳಿ}} \emph{caḷi}, native Dravidian (\textquotedblleft{}cold\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{kāla} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{culture}
Where Tamil and Malayalam just say \emph{kaalam} (\textquotedblleft{}time/season,\textquotedblright{} itself ultimately Sanskrit-derived too, but assimilated long ago as ordinary vocabulary), Kannada's word for spring, \textbf{\kn{ವಸಂತ} \kn{ಋತು}}, keeps \textbf{both} halves visibly Sanskrit — \emph{vasanta} the season-name, \emph{ṛtu} the very word for \textquotedblleft{}season.\textquotedblright{} Summer, rain, and cold, by contrast, are built on native Dravidian roots (\emph{bēsige}, \emph{maḷe}, \emph{caḷi}).

And as with Tamil and Malayalam: it's \textbf{\kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ}} (\emph{maḷegāla}, the rains) that shapes Karnataka's agricultural year the most, not a clean four-way Western split.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}bēsige\textquotedblright{} — summer, native
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}maḷegāla\textquotedblright{} — the rains
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}caḷigāla\textquotedblright{} — the cold season, native
  \item \emph{Say it:} the double loan — \textquotedblleft{}vasanta ṛtu\textquotedblright{} — both halves Sanskrit
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kappu biḷi kempu nīli}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does \kn{ವಸಂತ} \kn{ಋತು} differ from the Tamil/Malayalam spring-word? (\textbf{Both halves are Sanskrit} — \emph{vasanta} and \emph{ṛtu}, \textquotedblleft{}season\textquotedblright{} itself — where Tamil/Malayalam just add the long-assimilated \emph{kaalam}.) Which season actually shapes Karnataka's year most? (\textbf{\kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ}}, the rains.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anusvara]{\kn{◌ಂ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S123-sign-anusvara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಚ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ಂ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ಂ}} — \emph{a nasal, ridden on the syllable before it}.

It is a \textbf{nasal}, written as a mark rather than as a letter. It rides on the syllable before it and turns the end of it nasal.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{◌ಂ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}} \emph{santōṣa} — joy / pleased to meet you
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}} \emph{ondu} — one
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟು}} \emph{eṇṭu} — eight
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}} \emph{ombattu} — nine
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌ಂ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{◌ಂ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{◌ಂ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{◌ಂ} three times, humming the nasal at the end of the syllable as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{◌ಂ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{◌ಂ}? What does it add to the syllable before it? (\textbf{A nasal.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[6]{\kn{೬} — the digit for āru}

\label{lesson:KA-S145-digit-six}



\begin{quote}
Before the new shape: \textbf{\kn{೫}} — which number is it?

One digit this time, and you already know its name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{೬}}
\textbf{\kn{೬}} — \textbf{6}, the digit for \textbf{\kn{ಆರು}} (\emph{āru}), \textquotedblleft{}six\textquotedblright{}.

A digit carries no sound of its own — it stands for a number, and you read it aloud with the word you learned when you learned to count.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{೬} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{೬} and follow its line. Copy the shape in front of you — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what you can see needs no such source.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the digits you have met, and name each one aloud
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{೧}  ·  \kn{೨}  ·  \kn{೩}  ·  \kn{೪}  ·  \kn{೫}  ·  \kn{೬}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}āru\textquotedblright{} as you point at \kn{೬}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number is \textbf{\kn{೬}}? (\textbf{6} — \emph{āru}, \kn{ಆರು}.) Name every digit you have met so far, in order.
\end{tcolorbox}
